passage: Last winter I took a big sheet of paper and drew three columns: top rank, middling rank, miss. Suraj Sir, our physics teacher, had told us to try it, and I rolled my eyes, because planning for a miss felt like inviting one. Under top rank I wrote the college I dreamed about. It felt strange, even a little sad, to write that column. But when I finished, my chest felt looser. The night before results I slept, and I hadn't expected to. — Parveen

passage:
Class 12 mentor's note, entrance exam guidance

Chinmay came to see me in November, quite anxious. He said, "If I don't get the top rank, everything collapses." We did an exercise instead of a pep talk.

He drew three boxes on the board: "Top rank", "Middle rank", "Miss". Under each, he listed what he would do. Top rank: the state engineering college he wanted. Middle rank: a good private college his cousin Maria had attended, with a known scholarship. Miss: a gap year with a part-time job and a retake, or a diploma course with lateral entry.

He looked at the board for a long time. Then he said, "So missing isn't the end. It's just box three."

I asked him to show the plan to his parents that week. His mother emailed me the next day to say they had agreed on the list. He seems steadier in class now.

qa.q: What were the three boxes Chinmay drew?
How did Chinmay feel before the exercise?
qa.a: He felt anxious and afraid, believing everything would collapse if he missed the top rank.

qa.q: What else could Chinmay do with the three-box plan?
qa.a: He could check application dates for the backup options now, so each box is ready to use if needed.

qa.q: How might Chinmay's mother see the plan?
qa.a: She probably feels relieved and reassured, seeing a clear list for every outcome rather than only one hope.

grounding: A mentor's note shows a student mapping three exam outcomes and listing a state college, a private option and a gap-year plan so a miss is not a collapse.

passage:
Tuesday night

I did the scary thing today. I planned for failure.

Lokesh bhaiya says planning for a miss doesn't jinx anything. It just means a miss won't flatten me. So I took a page and drew three columns.

If I get a top rank: the government college in our state, civil engineering. If I get a middle rank: the private college in Coimbatore, which is good and has a scholarship I checked. If I miss completely: a gap year, coaching again part-time, and a job at Appa's friend's printing press to save money. Or a polytechnic diploma, then lateral entry.

Writing the third column made my stomach hurt. But when I finished, the page looked less frightening than my head had felt.

I'm Tanvir. Tomorrow I'm showing it to Amma and Appa. Then I'm going back to studying for column one.

How did Tanvir feel writing the third column?
